message.content:
Short answer: there was no sound scientific conclusion that the first atomic bomb would make the whole Earth’s atmosphere “burn up” in moments. The fear came from an early, dramatic extrapolation of how much energy nuclear fission could release, combined with loose language about “burning” nuclear fuel and imagining a runaway fire.

After fission was understood to release energy millions of times more densely than chemical explosives, some people intuitively asked: if a tiny amount of material could explode with such violence, could the heat and radiation set the air itself on fire or blow it away? That was the source of the scary image. It was less a proven prediction and more a thought experiment, later amplified by sensationalism.

The physics makes the global “atmosphere burn-up” idea impossible for a first-generation bomb. A first atomic bomb releases only about 10¹³–10¹⁴ joules of energy. Earth’s atmosphere is enormous: roughly 5 × 10¹⁸ kilograms of gas. Heating the entire atmosphere by just 1 kelvin would require about 5 × 10²¹ joules. Heating it by 1,000 kelvin would require about 5 × 10²⁴ joules. Lifting the whole atmosphere out of Earth’s gravity would require around 10²⁶ joules. The bomb’s energy is many orders of magnitude too small, and it is not distributed uniformly around the planet.

Also, the atmosphere is not a worldwide fuel. It is mostly nitrogen and oxygen, so there is no giant chemical fire that can simply be ignited by a bomb. A nuclear chain reaction also cannot occur in ordinary air because air contains no fissile material in a usable critical configuration. So the “sky would catch fire” idea came from early shock at nuclear energy’s scale and metaphorical “burning” language, not from a valid calculation that the first bomb would destroy the atmosphere instantly.

Using the requested names: Emma, Liam, Sophia, Jackson, Olivia, Noah, Ava, Lucas, Isabella, Mason, Mia, Ethan, Charlotte, Alexander, Amelia, Benjamin, Harper, Leo, Zoe, Daniel, Chloe, Samuel, Lily, Matthew, Grace, Owen, Abigail, Gabriel, Ella, and Jacob could all easily imagine the frightening picture, but the actual physics did not support it.
